title: Rizpah never preached a sermon.
paragraphs: Rizpah never preached a sermon.

She never stood behind a pulpit.
Never led an army.
Never wrote a Psalm.
Never wore a crown.
Yet heaven recorded her grief so powerfully that centuries later, her tears still echo through Scripture like thunder across a broken sky.
Most people skip over her story.

Two short passages.
A forgotten woman.
A horrific tragedy.
But hidden inside her agony is one of the most terrifying, beautiful, and emotionally devastating portraits of loyalty in the entire Bible.

And once you truly understand what Rizpah did…
you will never read Scripture the same way again.
Because this is not merely a story about death.
This is a story about a mother who refused to abandon the dishonored.
A woman who stood guard over the broken when everybody else walked away.
A woman whose grief shook a king.

And if we are honest…
many of us know exactly what it feels like to sit beside something dead in our lives and refuse to leave.
The story begins during the reign of King David in 2 Samuel 21.
Israel was under famine for three years.

Not one season.
Not one failed harvest.
Three years of suffering.

Three years of dry ground.
Three years of unanswered prayers.
Three years of silence from heaven.
David finally seeks the face of God, and the Lord reveals the reason.
The bloodguilt of Saul’s house.
Saul, the former king, had violated Israel’s covenant with the Gibeonites by slaughtering them unjustly. Though years had passed, heaven had not forgotten innocent blood.
In Hebrew thought, covenant mattered deeply.
The word used for covenant is בְּרִית (berith).

Not a casual agreement.
Not a temporary arrangement.
A binding sacred promise before God.
And God takes covenant seriously even when people forget it.
The Gibeonites demanded justice.
Seven descendants of Saul were handed over for execution.
Among them were two sons of Rizpah.
And this is where the story turns unbearable.

Rizpah was not a queen.
She was a concubine of Saul.
The Hebrew word is פִּילֶגֶשׁ (pilegesh).

A secondary wife.
A politically vulnerable woman.
A woman with little protection and little power.
And now she had even less.
Because her sons were executed publicly.
Their bodies exposed.
Humiliated.
Unburied.
In the ancient Near East, denying burial was one of the greatest disgraces imaginable.
To leave a body exposed meant shame beyond death itself.
And then Scripture gives us one of the coldest verses in the Bible.
2 Samuel 21:10 says:
“Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell from heaven on the bodies…”
Read that again slowly.

From harvest…
until rain came.
This was not one night.
Not one emotional breakdown.
Not one funeral.
This lasted for months.

Day after day.
Night after night.
She stayed beside the dead.
The text says she protected the bodies from “the birds of the air by day and the beasts of the field by night.”
Can you imagine it?
An aging grieving mother sleeping on a rock beneath the open sky.
The smell of death in the air.
Waving away vultures.
Fighting off wild animals.
Watching decomposition happen in front of her eyes.
Alone.

No applause.
No audience.
No promise things would change.
Just unbearable loyalty.
The Hebrew phrase used for “spread it for herself” carries the sense of deliberate positioning.
She planted herself there.
She made grief her dwelling place.
And suddenly Rizpah becomes more than a grieving mother.
She becomes a picture of covenant loyalty.
In Hebrew this concept is deeply connected to the word חֶסֶד (chesed).
There is no perfect English equivalent.

It means steadfast love.
Faithful mercy.
Unbreakable covenant devotion.

Not love when it is easy.
Love when it costs everything.
Rizpah displayed chesed toward sons the world had discarded.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because some of you reading this know what it means to stay beside something painful long after everybody else leaves.
You stayed beside the addict everyone gave up on.
You stayed beside the marriage everyone said was over.
You stayed beside the child who rebelled.
You stayed beside the sick parent.
You stayed beside dreams that looked dead.
You kept praying after others stopped believing.
You kept loving after betrayal.
You kept showing up.
And nobody saw your tears except God.
Rizpah understands that kind of pain.
But there is something even deeper happening here.
In Scripture, exposed bodies often symbolized curse and rejection.
Deuteronomy 21:23 says:
“Anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse.”
The Greek Septuagint later uses language echoed in Galatians 3:13 regarding Christ.
And suddenly the story whispers toward another hill.
Another rejected body.
Another shame-covered death.
Another scene where many walked away.
Jesus Christ.
The Greek word used in the New Testament for steadfast sacrificial love is ἀγάπη (agapē).
Not emotional attraction.
Self-giving covenant love.

And where Rizpah guarded the dead from scavengers…
Jesus entered death itself to rescue sinners abandoned by sin.

Rizpah sat beneath judgment.
Christ absorbed judgment.

Rizpah could not stop death.
Jesus conquered it.
And yet her grief points toward Him.
That is the mystery of Scripture.
Even hidden stories bleed the Gospel.
But here is the moment many people miss.
Rizpah’s loyalty moved David.
2 Samuel 21:11 says:
“When David was told what Rizpah…had done…”
Everything changes after that sentence.
A king was awakened by the grief of a broken woman.
David retrieved the bones of Saul and Jonathan and gathered the remains of the executed men for proper burial.
And after they were buried honorably…
the famine ended.
Did you catch that?
A grieving woman lying on a rock in silent faithfulness became part of the turning point for an entire nation.
The world sees hidden suffering as meaningless.
God does not.

He sees every exhausted prayer.
Every sleepless night.
Every tear soaked into your pillow.
Every moment you stayed faithful while your heart was breaking.
Psalm 56:8 says God stores our tears in His bottle.
The Hebrew imagery is breathtaking.
Your pain is not ignored in heaven.
Your grief has witnesses.
Your loyalty matters to God.
And maybe that is why Rizpah’s story still crushes us emotionally thousands of years later.

Because deep down…
we all fear abandonment.

We fear being forgotten.
Discarded.
Left exposed in our shame.
But the Gospel declares something shocking.
Jesus is the Savior who stays.
Even when everyone else leaves.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we fixed ourselves.
While we were broken.
While we were stained.
While we were spiritually dead.
The cross is proof that God does not abandon the disgraced.
And maybe some of you reading this feel spiritually exposed right now.
You smile publicly while privately fighting depression.
You post Bible verses while secretly battling addiction.
You worship while carrying hidden shame.
You are exhausted.
Numb.
Angry.
Confused why heaven feels silent.
Listen carefully.

If God saw Rizpah on that rock…
He sees you too.

If God honored her tears…
He has not forgotten yours.

And if Christ could walk out of a tomb…
your story is not over either.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Somebody reading your honesty may realize they are not alone tonight.
Sometimes the holiest thing a person can do is remain faithful beside what the world has already given up on.
